meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas. doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.title: The ratio of macronutrients, not caloric intake, dictates cardiometabolic health, aging, and longevity in ad libitum-fed mice

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: Lifespan and cardiometabolic health were determined not by caloric intake but by the protein:carbohydrate ratio; a low protein ratio was associated with lower hepatic mTOR activation.
data.abstract_excerpt: The fundamental questions of what represents a macronutritionally balanced diet and how this maintains health and longevity remain unanswered. Here, the Geometric Framework, a state-space nutritional modeling method, was used to measure interactive effects of dietary energy, protein, fat, and carbohydrate on food intake, cardiometabolic phenotype, and longevity in mice fed one of 25 diets ad libitum. Food intake was regulated primarily by protein and carbohydrate content.

extracted_findings.intervention: Dietary – 25 diets varying protein:carb:fat, ad libitum
extracted_findings.effect: Macronutrient ratio (low protein, high carb), not calorie intake, optimizes cardiometabolic health and longevity
extracted_findings.dose: 25 ad libitum diets differing in protein (5%–60%), fat (16%–75%), carbohydrate (16%–75%), and energy (8, 13, or 17 kJ/g of food) fed over a lifetime
extracted_findings.effect_size: Median lifespan increased by approximately 30% (from 95 to 125 weeks) as the protein-to-carbohydrate ratio decreased; not influenced by total calorie intake
